title: Exact $T$-counts of Toffoli layers from an isotropy bound
abstract: The $T$-count is the dominant cost of fault-tolerant Clifford+$T$ computation. We prove that a layer of $m$ disjoint CCZ gates, the diagonal core of a parallel Toffoli layer, needs exactly $6m+1$ $T$ gates in every Hadamard-free Clifford+$T$ circuit with clean ancillas. Campbell and Howard gave the matching construction. To our knowledge this is the first proof that it is optimal for general $m$ (for $m=1$ the value $7$ is classical, and Campbell and Howard state the value $13$ at $m=2$). On every controlled unitary the same floor comes within one of their exact count, and it recovers their $4m+3$ for a fan-out of $m$ Toffolis from one control. The proof rests on an isotropy constraint: for a pure-cubic phase, the vectors recording which $T$ gates touch each qubit span a totally isotropic subspace. In general the constraint gives the isotropy floor $δ\ge2(n-d^{\ast})-r$ for every diagonal level-three gate, computed from the phase polynomial in polynomial time. The floor is never below stabilizer nullity $ν$, which equals $n-d^{\ast}$ on this class, and a separate parity argument raises it to $2ν+1$ on non-Clifford pure-cubic gates. On the output of the TODD optimizer for the $24$ benchmark circuits it completes, the floor certifies $193$ of its $311$ merged phase-polynomial blocks optimal for their Hadamard layering ($186$ to $193$ across five optimizer seeds), against $113$ for nullity. The floor also holds, under stated conditions, for circuits whose only internal Hadamards form unitarily uncomputed temporary AND blocks, while under adaptive feedforward only $t\geν$ is proved.
summary: This paper provides a rigorous proof establishing the exact minimum T-gate count required for implementing layers of CCZ gates in fault-tolerant quantum computation. It introduces and utilizes the 'isotropy floor' as a powerful mathematical tool to derive these lower bounds. The work is significant because it establishes optimality for general layer sizes, advancing the theoretical understanding of quantum circuit resource costs.
main_problem: The paper aims to determine the minimum T-count, which is the dominant cost, for implementing fault-tolerant Clifford+T quantum computations.
main_result: It proves that a layer of $m$ disjoint CCZ gates requires exactly $6m+1$ T gates, establishing a new optimal lower bound for general $m$.
method: The core method involves deriving a lower bound called the 'isotropy floor' ($\delta$) by analyzing the phase polynomial of diagonal gates using isotropy constraints.
model_or_system: The study focuses on Hadamard-free Clifford+T quantum circuits utilizing clean ancillas, specifically analyzing the cost associated with parallel Toffoli layers (CCZ gates).

important_parameters: The bound depends on the order-$\le 3$ moments of the phase polynomial, and the results are parameterized by the number of qubits ($n$) and the layer size ($m$).
main_assumptions: The primary model assumes Hadamard-free circuits with clean ancillas; the bound is derived from an isotropy constraint on the phase polynomial.
figures_summary: The notes mention figures summarizing the end-to-end argument for the isotropy floor, specifically showing the CCZ case yielding a T-count of 7.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from analyzing a single gate (CCZ) to establishing general lower bounds (Isotropy Floor) using moment tensors, and then extending these results to layers of gates.
why_interesting: While focused on gate complexity, the rigorous mathematical techniques used to derive resource bounds (like the isotropy floor) are highly relevant to understanding the resource scaling in complex quantum simulations or quantum error correction codes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: The 6m + 1 construction, drawn at m = 2: bracketing the second block onto a qubit of the first removes one gate, so the pair uses thirteen Ts where two independent blocks would use fourteen. The circuit restores its wires and implements CCZabcCCZdef (checked by simulation, Appendix L).

Figure 3: How sharing lowers the T-count. Two CCZ blocks both act on wire 0, and their circuits run one after the other. Each block places one of its Ts on wire 0 itself. Wire 0 is only ever a CNOT control, so it carries x0 throughout and the two boxed Ts act on the same parity. They combine into S, a Clifford gate, and the pair is removed.

Figure 4: Sharing qubits interpolates the cost of a CCZ layer, and the radical dimension measures the position of a layer in that interpolation. Disjoint blocks give d = 0 on n = 3m qubits and cost 6m + 1 (Theorem 40). Fanning every block out of one shared control keeps d = 0 but drops n to 2m + 1, so the cost falls to exactly 4m + 3 (Theorem 43); each single-qubit merge saves two T-gates (Corollary 45). Sharing a full pair sends d to n −3, and the layer is Clifford-equivalent to a single gate, δ = 7, for every m (Remark 49).
Figure 5: The standard ancilla-based CCZ circuit, built from a temporary AND on one clean ancilla, with the quantities of Remark 88.
Figure 6: Dilation. Left, the outcome of measuring a selects a correction C. Right, the measurement is deferred and C becomes controlled-C, one Clifford level higher.
